title: Statins: the next step in adjuvant therapy for sepsis?
text_summary: 本文发表于Intensive Care Medicine（2006，IF=27.1），是一篇讨论他汀能否成为脓毒症辅助治疗的社论。文章回顾他汀除降脂外的多效性，包括抑制甲羟戊酸通路、降低CRP和炎症细胞因子、调节免疫反应、改善内皮功能、增加一氧化氮生物利用度以及减弱组织因子、凝血酶和纤溶失衡。健康志愿者内毒素挑战、动物感染模型和回顾性临床研究提示既往或持续使用他汀可能降低严重感染、脓毒症和死亡风险，但证据受适应证偏倚、药物种类与剂量差异、危重患者药代动力学和停药效应影响。作者强调目前观察性结果不足以确立疗效，需要前瞻性随机对照试验确定适用人群、给药时机、药物选择和安全性，尤其关注肝肌毒性及与重症用药的相互作用。

Intensive Care Med (2006) 32:11–14
DOI 10.1007/s00134-005-2860-5 EDITORIAL
Armand Mekontso-Dessap
Christian Brun-Buisson Statins: the next step in adjuvant therapy
for sepsis?
Received: 21 October 2005
Accepted: 26 October 2005
Published online: 10 November 2005

This editorial refers to the articles http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/
s00134-005-2743-9 and http://dx.doi.org./10.1007/s00134-005-
2859-y.
A. Mekontso-Dessap · C. Brun-Buisson ( ))
Service de R/C216animation M/C216dicale,

e-mail: christian.brun-buisson@hmn.aphp.fr
Keywords Statin · Sepsis · HMG-CoA ·
Adjuvant therapy
Statins are powerful hypolipemic drugs with pleiotropic
effects and have been shown to improve survival in the
primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerosis in
numerous large randomized clinical trials [1–6]. Inter-
estingly, in many of these trials, their beneficial clinical
impact included noncoronary events. For example, statin
therapy was consistently associated with decreased C-
reactive protein (CRP) levels in recent human clinical
trials, although the magnitude of this effect varied be-
tween drugs [7].
By inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A
(HMG-CoA) reductase and the mevalonate pathway to
cholesterol, statins reduce not only cholesterol but also the
production of several of its nonsteroidal isoprenoid pre-
cursor intermediates [8], which are necessary to membrane
anchor proteins critical to the binding of signaling proteins
involved in various cell functions. Several cellular
and animal models demonstrate the pleiotropic activity
of statins, including antiinflammatory and antioxidative
properties, immunomodulatory effects, improvement in
endothelial function, reduction in blood thrombogenicity,
and increased nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability. Some or
all of these effects may account for a substantial potential
impact of statins on the complex pro- and antiinflamma-
tory sequence of events occurring during sepsis.
Statins affect the production of many acute phase re-
actants, including CRP, which is produced in the liver
under stimulation by cytokines (IL-1 and IL-6). In
nonatherosclerotic huCRP transgenic mice, statins de-
creased basal and IL-1 b-induced plasma huCRP levels
independently of cholesterol lowering and of an effect on
IL-6 production [9], likely reflecting downregulation of
hepatocyte responsiveness to this cytokine. Simvastatin
has been shown to reduce inflammation in atherosclerotic
plaques and cytokine production in blood mononuclear
cells [10]. These studies suggest that the inhibition of
sterol or nonsterol derivatives from mevalonate bio-
transformation plays a major role in the in vivo antiin-
flammatory action of statins, with inhibition of lipopoly-
saccharide-induced leukocyte recruitment and of the
production of various cytokines [11]. However, the in
vitro effect of hydrophilic (pravastatin) and hydrophobic
(atorvastatin, lovastatin, and simvastatin) drugs on cyto-
kine production is not identical.
Statin treatment attenuates the inflammatory as well as
the procoagulant processes during acute lipopolysaccha-
ride (LPS) challenge. In a double-blind, placebo-con-
trolled study of 20 healthy, male subjects, a 4-day sim-
vastatin pretreatment significantly suppressed the in-
creases in hsCRP and MCP-1—both known inducers of
tissue factor (TF)—observed after LPS challenge [12].
Statins appear to reduce procoagulant activity at different
stages of the coagulation cascade, including TF activity,
conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, and thrombin
activity. The inhibitory effect of statins on the mevalonate
pathway probably regulates the synthesis of TF, tissue
plasminogen activator (tPA), and plasminogen activator
inhibitor-1 precursor (PAI-1), and may also control the
12
generation and activity of thrombin [13]. By altering the
levels and activities of tPA and PAI-1, statins also appear
to stimulate fibrinolysis. Experimental and clinical studies
have recently suggested that statins also induce favorable
lipid-independent effects on hemostasis. For example, the
expression and functional activity of human endothelial
thrombomodulin–of which the acquired deficiency is of
particular pathophysiologic significance in sepsis and
related disorders–is strongly increased by atorvastatin and
simvastatin [14].
On the hemodynamic side, statins may contribute to
improved outcome in sepsis by preserving vascular re-
sponsiveness. In a randomized, placebo-controlled study
of 20 healthy volunteers, simvastatin was shown to pre-
serve the forearm blood flow response to norepinephrine
and to acetylcholine after LPS challenge [15]. Similar
results were obtained in animals [16]. During sepsis,
production of TNFalpha and IFNgamma reduce endo-
thelial constitutive NO synthase (cNOS) expression and
function, but NO increases as a result of inducible NO
synthase (iNOS) overexpression via activation of tran-
scriptional factors STAT-1 and NF-kappaB [17], likely
contributing to vasoplegic shock [18]. A time-dependent
increase in nitrate plasma concentration occurs in animals
after LPS challenge, which is reduced in animals pre-
treated with simvastatin or cerivastatin [16, 19] and is
associated with improved survival [19]. Statin pretreat-
ment was also found to decrease cytokine-stimulated
transcription factor activation and iNOS expression in the
endothelium [16].
In addition to peripheral vascular effects, statins may
also alleviate sepsis-associated myocardial dysfunction.
In a mouse cecal ligation and perforation (CLP) model,
pretreatment with simvastatin was associated with a mean
survival time close to four times that of untreated mice
[20]. This dramatic improvement was associated with a
complete preservation of cardiac function and hemody-
namic status, which were severely impaired in untreated
CLP mice. In a subsequent study, the same group [21]
found that statin therapy initiated at 6 h post-CLP was
also associated with a 40% prolonged survival time when
either atorvastatin, pravastatin, or simvastatin, but not
fluvastatin, was used.
The above brief overview of in vitro and experimental
studies, including several human studies, strongly sug-
gests that statin pretreatment may attenuate the inflam-
matory response, prevent vascular and endothelial dys-
function, and even prevent myocardial dysfunction during
sepsis. However, few studies have tested statin therapy
administered after the infectious challenge.
A few clinical studies have been published recently in
support of the first hypothesis. Almog et al. [22] con-
ducted a prospective observational cohort study to de-
termine the impact of statin pretreatment on the occur-
rence of severe sepsis in infected patients. Of 361 patients
with confirmed acute bacterial infection, 82 (23%) had
been receiving statins for at least 4 weeks prior to their
admission. The crude mortality rate was low and did not
differ significantly between the two groups (3.7% vs.
8.6%, P=0.21), but severe sepsis developed in 2.4% and
19% of patients, respectively, in the statin and no-statin
group (risk ratio 0.13; 95% CI, 0.03–0.52), and the ICU
admission rate was 12.2% for the no-statin group com-
pared with only 3.7% of the statin group ( P=0.025). In
another retrospective review of 388 patients with bacter-
emia, Liappis et al [23] reported a significant reduction in
both overall (6% vs. 28%, P=0.002) and attributable
(3% vs. 20%, P=0.010) mortality among patients taking
statins at the time of admission compared with patients
not taking statins. The survival benefit persisted after
adjustment for prognostic factors in a multivariate anal-
ysis (odds ratio 7.6; 95% CI, 1.01–57.5).
Two cohort studies in this issue of Intensive Care
Medicine also address the potential impact of statin
therapy in sepsis [24, 25]. Kruger et al. [25], using a
similar study design to Liappis et al. [23], retrospectively
analyzed a cohort of 438 patients with clinically signifi-
cant bacteremia admitted over a 4-year period to two
hospitals in Australia. Only 66 (15%) of patients were
receiving statins upon admission, 56 (85%) of whom
continued statin therapy during their hospital stay. Crude
28-day mortality was significantly lower in statin-treated
patients (10.6% vs. 23.1%; odds ratio 0.4, 0.17–0.90),
although there was no difference in ICU admission rates
between the two groups. The difference persisted when
examining bacteremia-related deaths and after adjustment
for age, immunodepression, and infection with E. coli ,
which differed significantly between groups. The authors
noted that the difference in mortality was essentially due
to patients in whom statin therapy was maintained,
whereas mortality appeared higher in those in whom
therapy was discontinued. However, the latter subgroup
was very small and this analysis was uncontrolled, so no
conclusion can be derived from this observation. Inherent
to such retrospective studies–similarly to the previous one
by Liappis et al.–is the inability to thoroughly control for
known and unknown imbalances between groups (for
instance, overall severity and underlying diseases). Not
unexpectedly, patients on statins were older and had more
comorbidities and chronic organ dysfunctions, but they
had less immunodepression and a lesser acute severity
with a lower prevalence of shock (7.6% vs. 17.5%,
P=0.13). Although this study must again be viewed as
hypothesis-generating, it still provides one more piece of
evidence in favor of a protective effect of statins in sepsis.
How, then, should the negative findings reported by
Fernandez et al. [24], also appearing in this issue, be in-
terpreted? These authors took a different approach, ex-
amining retrospectively whether a selected group of ICU
patients at high risk of infection (that is, those receiving
mechanical ventilation for longer than 96 h) would have a
lower rate of ICU-acquired infection and lower mortality
13
when receiving prior and ongoing statin therapy ( n=38)
than their counterparts not receiving prior statin therapy
(n=400). Again, patients receiving statins were older (by
10 years) and had more comorbidities, chronic organ
failures, and higher APACHE II scores. Although the
infection rate was nonsignificantly lower (29% vs. 38%,
P=0.3) in statin recipients, they actually had a higher
hospital mortality rate (61% vs. 42%, P=0.03), even after
adjustment on APACHE II predicted risk of death. The
authors rightfully conclude that statin therapy was prob-
ably associated with (and reflected) comorbidities rather
than an increased risk of death per se and that adjustment
by APACHE II scores was likely insufficient to account
for these. In fact, it appears questionable to adjust on the
risk of death predicted from an admission severity score
in a selected population defined by an ICU stay of 4 days
or more when associated conditions have a major impact
on outcome; in this regard, whether limitation of therapy
occurred was also not reported. In addition, the small
subgroup of patients receiving statins (8.7% of the cohort)
makes outcome comparisons hazardous when not thor-
oughly controlled for, and a case-control study might
have been more convincing. Finally, the incidence of
severe sepsis or shock in infected patients was not re-
ported, whereas experimental and clinical studies suggest
that statins have the potential to attenuate or prevent the
severity of sepsis rather than to prevent infection itself.
The available evidence today suggests that the poten-
tial for statins as adjuvant therapy for sepsis should be
further tested. Given their pleiotropic effects related to
many pathophysiologic determinants of sepsis, statin
therapy could well be the next step in the search for ad-
juvant therapy. However, the relative importance of prior
and ongoing statin therapy needs to be more clearly de-
fined, and more studies testing the effects of statins ad-
ministered at the onset of sepsis are needed, as well as
studies on the differential effects of the various drugs
belonging to this family.

image_summary: 第1页：Intensive Care Medicine社论首页，介绍他汀作为脓毒症辅助治疗的理论基础，重点讨论降脂之外的抗炎、抗氧化、免疫调节、内皮保护和一氧化氮相关作用。
第2页：继续综述他汀对凝血、组织因子、凝血酶、tPA/PAI-1和血小板过程的影响，并评述内毒素挑战、动物模型及感染临床观察证据。
第3页：讨论既往他汀使用与脓毒症发生率和病死率降低的观察性研究，同时分析混杂偏倚、药物差异、危重症药代动力学和安全性问题，呼吁随机试验。
第4页：参考文献页，列出他汀心血管试验、抗炎与抗凝机制、感染动物模型、脓毒症观察研究和安全性相关文献。
